body:
T113's failed-login limiter produced TWO confirmed auth-bypasses in successive P5 rounds, and the second was introduced by the fix for the first. The current state is safe against both, but the policy it settles on is a DECISION about what the door promises under attack, and that is Myk's, not the model's.

WHAT SHIPPED (safe, and the reasoning is in login-locks.ts): no live lock is ever evictable — every eviction rule over live locks is steerable, because taking the nearest-to-expire takes the first victim's lock and taking the furthest takes the victim's the moment their own is newest. An attempt the table cannot account for is REFUSED before the password comparison, so guessing is bounded. `saturatedFor` is that pre-check.

THE COST, stated plainly: a caller who pays maxFailures × maxTracked attempts (2560 at the shipped defaults, about a minute) can shut the HTML LOGIN DOOR for every name the table does not already hold, until the locks drain (15 minutes). The bearer-token doors are untouched. The recovery is waiting out lockMs or `loam user unlock --all` from the box. A RESTART DOES NOT clear it — round 7 found that claim false, and the claim is now exact. So it is a recoverable denial rather than a compromise.

SEPARATELY, and simpler: a caller who knows the username can hold that ONE name locked forever with five wrong passwords per fifteen minutes. That is inherent to a username-keyed limiter, and a source-keyed one is worse behind a funnel where every request is 127.0.0.1.

THE DECISION FOR MYK — three options, and the model recommends (b):
(a) Keep it. A remote party can deny the browser login; the API stays open; recovery is on the box.
(b) Replace DENY with DELAY: per-username exponential backoff, capped, that never refuses a correct password. Nobody can ever be locked out, and guessing collapses to a few attempts per second against the global hash budget. This removes the whole lockout class rather than trading it around. It does weaken a hard stop, so it is a promise change and needs Myk's word.
(c) Take the login door off the public internet and reach it over the tailnet only. Removes the exposure rather than the flaw — but the OAuth consent page (T114) must be publicly reachable for a connector to work, and it shares the origin, so this needs a path-scoped funnel to be real.

RAILS, whichever is chosen, both sides: guessing is bounded AND a legitimate correct password is never permanently refused. The current rails are `test/server/login-limit.test.ts` — the saturation refusal and the flood-cannot-evict pair.

MYK'S DECISION (2026-07-27, chat): OPTION (b) — replace DENY with DELAY. So: no hard lock. A
per-username backoff makes each further failure more expensive, capped, and A CORRECT PASSWORD IS
NEVER REFUSED. That removes the whole lockout class rather than trading it around — nobody,
including a stranger who knows the username, can shut the operator out. Guessing collapses to a few
attempts per second against the global concurrent-hash budget.

WHAT THAT REPLACES: the lock itself — `lockedUntil`, the 429-before-hash refusal, and
`saturatedFor` — because the saturation problem DISSOLVES. There is no scarce lock left to protect,
so no eviction rule can be steered and a full table cannot become an off switch. Both bypasses this
ticket records were bugs in machinery that option (b) deletes. `loam user unlock` keeps its meaning:
clear this name's accumulated delay. `loam user unlock --all` keeps its meaning too.

THE COST, named: an attacker can make the operator's own login SLOW (up to the cap per attempt)
by accumulating failures against their username. Slow is not shut, and that is the whole trade.

RAILS, both sides, non-negotiable:
(a) a correct password is admitted after ANY number of prior failures — the whole point, and the
    rail that would go red if a lock crept back in
(b) the delay grows with failures and is capped, so it cannot become a denial by another name
(c) a flood against one name does not slow a DIFFERENT name's login
(d) concurrent attempts cannot reset or lose the accumulated delay (the lost-update shape that has
    already bitten this file once)
(e) the delay is read from a MONOTONIC clock, so a wall-clock step backwards cannot erase it
(f) a delayed attempt still costs the attacker a connection slot but must not exhaust the server:
    the concurrent-login cap is asserted with delays in flight


CORRECTION (2026-07-27): the eviction tie-break is fewest failures and among those the NEWEST, not the oldest. An earlier sentence here said oldest. That is wrong for the reason the rail now pins: a flood's fresh rows and an operator's established row can hold the same count, and evicting the oldest of an equal count hands the flood the operator's accumulated wait.

RAIL OWNERSHIP: `test/server/login-limit.test.ts` moves from T113's declared rails to this ticket's, because this ticket replaces what that file asserts. T113 keeps its other seven. The move is authorized deliberately — a rail frozen by a landed ticket would make the CI backstop refuse the PR that legitimately rewrites it.
title: The login limiter's saturation policy is a decision, not a repair — Myk chooses what the door does under a flood
